draft.title: Dissolving ionic compounds
card: An ionic solid is a lattice of positive and negative ions held together by strong attraction. Water is a polar molecule, so it has a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end.
When an ionic solid is added to water, the slightly negative ends of water molecules attract the positive ions. The slightly positive ends attract the negative ions.
These attractions pull ions out of the lattice, and water molecules surround each ion. The ions are now hydrated and spread through the solution.
Some ionic compounds dissolve only slightly. Only a small amount of the solid breaks up into ions, and most stays as solid.
draft.remember: Water's polar ends pull ions from the lattice, and slightly soluble salts release only a few.

a.q: Sodium chloride dissolves in water. Which change describes what happens to the solid?
opts: Water molecules surround and separate the ions
Water molecules break the bonds inside each ion
Sodium and chlorine atoms form new covalent bonds
The solid melts into a liquid made of molecules
a.why: Polar water molecules attract the ions and pull them out of the lattice, so the ions end up surrounded by water. Ions are not broken apart, and no covalent bonds form between sodium and chlorine.
a.clue: Think about which ends of water attract which ions.

b.q: Silver chloride is added to water, and only a tiny amount of it dissolves. What does this show?
opts: Only a small amount of the solid separates into ions
The water molecules cannot attract any ions at all
The solid does not contain ions in a lattice
The ions that dissolve are no longer surrounded by water
b.why: A slightly soluble compound releases only a few ions into solution, while most stays as solid. Water can still attract ions, and the dissolved ions are surrounded by water molecules like any others.
b.clue: Slightly soluble does not mean not at all.

a.best: Water molecules surround and separate the ions

b.best: Only a small amount of the solid separates into ions
